newsitem.title: UK: London gold slips on fresh fears of IMF sales.
newsitem.headline: London gold slips on fresh fears of IMF sales.

text.p: Gold prices crumbled on Friday after a fresh report appeared about possible gold sales by the International Monetary Fund (IMF), but volumes were thin ahead of a three-day U.S. weekend.

Prices had been slipping for the past several days and gained a little added momentum from a newspaper report saying that the IMF was circulating a new plan to sell some of its gold stockpiles to finance debt relief to poor countries.
Bullion fixed in the afternoon at $386.45 per ounce, 80 cents down from the morning setting. Spot gold closed in Europe at $386.35, down $1.90 from Thursday.
For several weeks prices had been moving higher from early July lows around $380, but stalled around $390 recently and drifted lower over the past few days.
The New York Times said on Friday the IMF had sent a new plan to member governments this week regarding the sale of some of its $40 billion in bullion holdings.
IMF member countries have long been wrangling over such a plan and failed in June at the Group of Seven countries meeting in Lyon, France to agree on a proposal to sell five percent of its stocks.
The G-7 countries -- the United States, Japan, Germany, Britain, France, Italy and Canada -- postponed any decision until the autumn.
Bullion dealers said there did not appear to be anything substantially new in the newspaper report, but it affected sentiment since it reminded the market that sales may be drawing near.
"Prices moved because this time maybe people think it's really going to happen and also the market's been so quiet," a dealer said.
Silver also lost ground, breaking below its trading range for the past 10 days and closing in London six cents weaker at $5.16 per ounce.
Platinum also caught the chill and finished in Europe at $395.40 an ounce, down $3.90 from Thursday. The fall interrupted an uptrend that started in early July.
Palladium, however, remained little changed, closing only 50 cents lower at $125.50 per ounce.
Analysts said a newspaper report that Russia had closed its diamond and precious metals sales agency should have little affect on the platinum and palladium markets.
"I don't think it (the agency's closure) is a fundamental change," said Michael Steel, market research director at Johnson Matthey.

The report in the Financial Times said responsibility for Russia's precious metals stockpile might fall under the control of the Finance Ministry, but Steel said the ministry already had influence on the agency's sales.
